stories.title: EU 'opening door' for Canada to become associate member
stories.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said ⁠the European Union is opening the door for Canada to become the first associate member, a status that does not exist under the bloc's ‌treaties. "Partnerships are ⁠a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system," Ms von der Leyen ‌said in her annual State of the ⁠European Union address in ‌Strasbourg. "We see the world with the same ⁠eyes: ‌from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we ⁠have stood together: on Ukraine, on ⁠defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all ... Europe and Canada believe in democracy." Turning to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is a special guest of the European Parliament this week and will address the chamber tomorrow, the European Commission President said the reality is the EU must "urgently re-imagine our partnerships" globally. To applause, she said "dear Mark, I would like to work with you, on opening the door on Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union". While the possible move was flagged earlier this week when Mr Carney said he wants a "unique alliance" with the EU, confirmation of an associate member plan is a significant development.

stories.title: 250,000 due to attend National Ploughing Championships
stories.summary: Around a quarter of a million people are expected to attend this year's National Ploughing Championships, which got under way in Screggan, Co Offaly today. President Catherine Connolly officially opened the event, which takes place against the backdrop of a number of prominent issues facing the country's farmers, including the rising cost of energy and climate change. This is the fifth time Screggan is hosting the event, which runs from today until Thursday. In her opening speech, President Catherine Connolly criticised a lack of action taken on tackling climate change, saying that as a collective, we have not taken proper action to address it. She also said the situation is starting to impact food production in Ireland, noting a major drop-off in the number of vegetable growers. The Championships are happening at a critical juncture for the country's farmers, who are facing into much uncertainty.

stories.title: Call for EU laws to ban trade with Israeli settlements
stories.summary: All of Ireland's 14 MEPs have signed a European Parliament-wide open letter to Ursula von der Leyen calling on her to introduce new EU laws banning any trade between Europe and illegal Israeli settlements. The letter, which has been signed by more than 100 of the European Parliament's 720 MEPs, was published a day before the European Commission president's state of the union address tomorrow and is targeted at placing pressure on her to take action. In the letter, MEPs say in their view it is time to "finally bring forward a legislative proposals to ban EU trade with Israel's illegal settlements in the occupied territories". Referencing British foreign minister Ed Miliband's decision last week to support a similar move, the letter continued: "Our citizens demand action. While our credibility on the international stage has already been damaged through inaction, a legislative proposals will be a positive step in the right direction. "We therefore urge the European Commission to propose the necessary regulation." The open letter follows similar correspondence in July by 71 MEPs, and a separate call in June by 460 former member state prime ministers, European commissioners, government ministers, ambassadors, MEPs and senior EU officials for tougher action by EU in response to what is happening in Gaza and the West Bank.

stories.title: Could cheap flights be about to get more expensive?
stories.summary: Analysis: The era of cheap flights isn't going to go overnight, but expect change if oil prices stay high and airlines keep trimming capacity to match For years, cheap flights have been one of the great bargains of European travel. Flying across the continent for €20 or €30 became normal, but that may be getting harder to sustain - and Ireland could be more exposed than most. Ryanair has trimmed its passenger target for the year to March 2027 from 216 million to 214 million, and warned that European short-haul fares could rise materially if oil prices remain high, particularly if less well-hedged competitors are forced to cut capacity. This warning has sharpened in recent days. Chief executive Michael O'Leary said on 10 September that winter fares could come in flat or only slightly higher, rather than falling as previously expected - with a much bigger increase possible if oil stays expensive into 2027. The mechanics are simple enough. Aircraft burn a lot of fuel, and fuel is one of an airline's biggest costs. The hard part is deciding how much of that can be passed on to passengers without losing them to someone cheaper. Low-cost carriers compete almost entirely on price: add €20 to a ticket overnight and some passengers simply won't travel. That's why airlines hedge fuel well in advance: locking in a price today for fuel they won't burn for months, so a spike doesn't hit all at once. The airline says 80% of its 2027 jet-fuel requirements are hedged at about $67 a barrel, about as belt-and-braces as fuel hedging gets. But the remaining fifth sits exposed to the open market, and it's already done real damage. In its July results, Ryanair said the price of that unhedged 20% had more than doubled to roughly $150 a barrel during the first quarter, pushing operating costs up 11% and dragging profit after tax down 34%. Ryanair's own results are a useful gauge of how fast a fuel spike can bite, even for the carrier with Europe's strongest hedging position. That's why the airline is pulling back rather than pushing through. Ryanair has cut roughly two million seats from its winter schedule, a move it says could shave €70 million to €100 million off its losses. The Financial Times  reported the cut is Ryanair's first significant winter capacity reduction since the pandemic - not a routine trim. Fewer seats can, in time, mean higher fares, particularly on routes where competition is thin to begin with.

stories.title: Iran rejects any talks with US after Trump remarks
stories.summary: Iran's security chief has rejected any talks with the United States after President Donald Trump said he was open to resuming discussions on the Middle East war. "Don't get distracted by the US president's mixed signals - from 'no negotiations' to 'we're ready to talk'," the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, posted on X. "The stakes around oil and the straits have changed. Damage control won't stop what's coming. No talks until Iran's conditions are met. Period!" he added. Yesterday, Mr Trump said he was open to holding talks with Iran, after weeks of saying it was too early to make a deal to end the war. stories.title: 2027 Irish Open moved to July date
stories.summary: Shane Lowry's expected defence of his Irish Open title will take place in an earlier slot in the calendar in 2027 with the K Club event to be held from 1 to 4 July. September has been the usual month for the national event in recent seasons, but with Adare Manor hosting the Ryder Cup from 17-19 September, it has been pushed back and will now be the first event on the DP World Tour's 'Closing Swing' series. The Kildare event will be held two weeks before the Open at St Andrew's, potentially making it a destination for some of the game's top players in a tune-up for the final major of the year. A number of events have returned to the DP World Tour schedule – the Hong Kong Open and Deutsche Bank Singapore Open, co-sanctioned with the Asian Tour, and the the Open de Portugal|Cascais-Lisboa, last played in 2020. The dates for the FedEx Open de France (9-12 September) and BMW PGA Championship (23-26 September) have also been changed due to the Ryder Cup. The Irish Open has had home winners for its last two seasons, Lowry winning by a record 11 strokes at Doonbeg last weekend and Rory McIlroy triumphing at the K Club in 2025.

stories.summary: All-Ireland SHC winning manager Liam Cahill will work with a much-changed backroom team for the 2027 season. In July it was announced that Cahill – who guided the Premier County to the Liam MacCarthy in 2025 – was to remain in place until 2029. Selectors Declan Laffan and TJ Ryan depart with Brian O'Meara and Sean O'Meara in place. Paul O'Brien will be a selector and offer coaching support with Aidan Stakelum also acting in a coaching support role. Angelo Walsh also leaves and strength and conditioning coach position with Kilkenny man John Murphy now taking on that role. Diarmuid Cahill, who recently stepped down as Longford boss, will be goalkeeping coach with Anne Marie Kennedy overseeing sports performance.

stories.title: St Pat's move top of the table after Dundalk demolition
stories.summary: St Patrick's Athletic moved top of the SSE Airtricity Men’s Premier Division table in style at Oriel Park with a thumping 4-0 victory over Dundalk. Stephen Kenny enjoyed some of his greatest title triumphs at the Louth stadium and this result will give Saints fans reasons to dream of another as they not only leapfrogged Shamrock Rovers at the summit but doubled their goal difference advantage to eight in the process. A first-half double from Aidan Keena and second-half goals from Ryan Sheridan and Ryan Edmondson means the Saints are closer than ever to a first league win since 2013. While Stephen Bradley’s side have a game in hand to restore their advantage, it is against a Bohemians team who will also feel they have a chance of finishing the campaign top of the pile for the first time since 2009. The home side started promisingly but an Aodh Dervin shot from distance that was well over was all they had to show for their efforts. By contrast, St Pat’s were slow to grow into the game but they did give a glimpse of their undoubted threat when Sheridan found Keena at the edge of the box on 14 minutes only for the striker to scuff rather tamely at Enda Minogue.

stories.title: Wall revitalised as Ireland target five wins this window
stories.summary: Ireland lock Dorothy Wall is injury-free and ready to hit the ground running as Ireland ramp up preparations for the WXV Global Series. The Tipperary woman featured in all five of Ireland's Six Nations games this year having made a successful return from injury, but now feels in a great place with a full pre-season under her belt. "Post-injury, I kind of went straight into a season, and having an actual pre-season to build up strength scores, explosiveness, etc, and to actually feel rested was kind of new for me. "I enjoyed that. I enjoyed the hard graft. I've really enjoyed getting more game stuff in in camp here, but it doesn't really feel like we've been out of the game either." Wall suffered an Achilles' tendon injury in the final Six Nations game of 2025, a 26-19 defeat away to Scotland. This meant she missed Ireland's Rugby World Cup tilt later that year but the 26-year-old insists she has no regrets. "I guess I can't regret an injury that wasn't my fault", she said.

stories.title: From Marvel Tokon to PAW Patrol – the latest games reviewed
stories.summary: We're well past the halfway mark of the year, and the gaming industry shows no signs of slowing down. Brand new releases across all genres ensure that no matter your interests or age, there’s something for everybody to enjoy. This past month is no exception, with giant franchises like Marvel and PAW Patrol back in force with some of their best work yet. And in true gaming fashion, we also have ambitious indies that prove some of the best games can come at us by surprise. These days, Marvel fans are spoilt for choice. Whether it's TV, film, comics, or games, you can jump into a brand-new experience featuring your favourite heroes and villains, all to the highest standard found in entertainment. Fighting Souls is no exception. This is the latest Marvel game, drawing on a limitless scope of superhero stories in the form of a 4vs4 tag-team fighter. Fast-paced and exploding with colour, this game has filled the drought fighting fans may have been experiencing, but is just as approachable to newcomers to the genre as well. The first thing you'll note about the game is the anime-like art style, which makes your screen an absolute joy to look at on a near-constant basis. Like some form of pixel eye-candy, every animation leads to a blast of colour, and detailed special effects with each move make every character’s array of abilities truly shine.

stories.title: Kielty: "The pressure of The Late Late Show is a privilege"
stories.summary: As he prepares for his fourth season of The Late Late Show, Patrick Kielty chats to Claire O'Mahony about settling into the show, changing audience expectations and learning to live in the moment. Patrick Kielty has a new way of describing his age, courtesy of a friend from Mayo who reached a landmark shortly before him. 'Britfic’, as he calls it, is inspired by the orange drink long advertised as "55", and Kielty needs little encouragement to explain the joke. "He turned around to me, same age as me, and he says, ‘You do know now we’re Britvic?’ I says, ‘What?’ He says, ‘55, 55!’" Kielty hit his mid-50s in January, although the birthday itself did not prompt any sudden reckoning or reappraisal. The reflection had already begun during a period in which his professional life remained under scrutiny, while his personal life experienced profound changes. His mother, Mary, died in March 2025, and his separation from his wife of 12 years, Cat Deeley, was announced the following July. As he gears up for a new season of The Late Late Show, he doesn't mention either loss, but acknowledges that recent years have altered the way he looks at the life immediately in front of him.

stories.title: Garda whistleblower unit members allege reforms undermined
stories.summary: Two people who handled protected disclosures made by Garda whistleblowers have themselves blown the whistle, alleging that reforms introduced to protect those who speak out have been undermined by senior management. The other two whistleblowers made protected disclosures to the office in recent years. The Garda Protected Disclosures Office was established in 2017 as part of reforms introduced to protect whistleblowers following a series of policing scandals, including the treatment of whistleblower Sergeant Maurice McCabe. The two key figures connected with the Garda Protected Disclosures Office are Dr Donal Corcoran and Rose Sweeney. Dr Corcoran, a serving, plain-clothes Garda for 25 years, was a permanently designated staff member in the Office up to January 2025. Ms Sweeney, a serving civilian principal officer, is head of the Garda National Youth Diversion Bureau, and acted as a part-time protected disclosures manager. Dr Corcoran, who holds qualifications in criminal justice, protected disclosures, law, ethics and mediation, and carried out the function of a facilitator of protected disclosures, ran the Office on behalf of protected disclosure managers and was regarded as its "institutional memory".

A post-mortem examination is due to be carried out at University Hospital Waterford. The driver of the van, a man aged in his 40s, was seriously injured and is being treated at Tipperary University Hospital in Clonmel. The road is currently closed for a technical examination, with local diversions in place.

stories.title: Cohesion funding key to EU solidarity, says minister
stories.summary: Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has said that cohesion funding remains one of the European Union's most effective expressions of solidarity. During Ireland's EU Presidency Mr Chambers is responsible for cohesion policy. Today he will welcome ministers and senior officials from across the European Union to discuss this issue in Dublin Castle. Cohesion funding is designed to reduce economic, social and territorial disparities across member states. It makes up more than one third of the current EU Budget amounting to €392bn, and it is one of the largest components of the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). Discussions are expected to focus on how cohesion policy can promote long-term competitiveness while reducing disparities between regions.

It is the first time since 2017 that a non-luxury company has claimed the top spot on the Paris bourse at the end of a trading day. Berenberg analyst Nick Anderson pointed to the lipstick effect - when the economic mood is bleak, it becomes easier to sell small treats rather than high-end handbags, shoes and dresses. "People simply can't afford to buy these expensive luxury items and instead are indulging in small luxuries like the proverbial lipstick to make themselves feel better," he said. L'Oreal's market capitalisation reached around €203 billion yesterday evening, according to LSEG data, with LVMH at €201 billion. stories.title: Some of Letby's murders could have been stopped - inquiry
stories.summary: British nurse Lucy Letby was able to murder seven newborns because of a "complete failure" to protect babies at the hospital at which she worked, and some of the deaths could have been avoided, the chair of an inquiry has said. Inquiry chair Kathryn Thirlwall criticised senior staff for not acting sooner, blaming dysfunctional management at the Countess of Chester Hospital in northern England and a basic lack of understanding of safeguarding. Letby, 36, was convicted in 2023 of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder six others, making her Britain's most prolific serial child killer of modern times. Prosecutors said Letby attacked the newborns by giving them an overdose of insulin, injecting them with air or force-feeding them milk between June 2015 and June 2016, in a case that shocked Britain and drew worldwide attention. But Letby, who was sentenced to life without parole and maintains she is innocent, has also been the subject of a growing campaign, backed by some medical experts and specialists, which has publicly questioned her convictions. Ms Thirlwall, who previously criticised "noise" around the case, did not address Letby's guilt or innocence in her report, dealing with the Countess of Chester Hospital's response and whether suspicions should have been raised earlier.

The first is Stephen Kenny's outfit are a direct rival who subsequently went on to follow up on the 2-0 victory with a four-goal thrashing of Dundalk that has put the Saints top on goal difference - albeit having played a game more. But the other worry for Rovers was the number of chances they gave up, highlighting defensive cracks that have been apparent during some of their chastening away days over the summer.

stories.title: Antrim clubs await fate as violence mars hurling clash
stories.summary: Antrim clubs Loughgiel and St John's will await their fate after violent scenes marred their senior hurling clash at Fr Healy Park. The group encounter, a repeat of last year’s county final, passed off without any major incident over the course of 63 minutes, with reigning champions St John’s losing out 3-14 to 0-30. Both sides advanced to the knockout stages in a game that saw just three yellow cards handed out. At the full-time whistle however tempers flared between both panels. Initially players and mentors on both sides clashed in the middle of the pitch, before footage from the ground shows how things escalated further with the violence spilling over into the crowd. The clubs will now await any proposed penalties resulting from the action.

stories.title: Blame me for Ireland v Israel games, not players - Martin
stories.summary: FAI Director of Football John Martin has spoken of the need to 'protect' Republic of Ireland players if they take part in the autumn UEFA Nations League matches against Israel, as he reiterated his stance that he'd prefer if the games did not have to be played. Heimir Hallgrimsson's team are scheduled to face Israel in Debrecen in Hungary on 27 September for the 'away' tie, before the return 'home' fixture on 4 October in Backa Topola, Serbia. In July an FAI motion in favour of proceeding with the Nations League double header against Israel was backed at an extraordinary general meeting. The delegates voted whether to endorse the FAI board's decision to fulfil the games, with the vote passing by 68% to 32%. Last month the FAI confirmed that there will be no tickets sold to Ireland supporters for the games with Ireland’s ‘home’ game being played behind closed door and only Israeli fans present for the September game. He said: "It's really hard on the players because I think someone said, ‘oh, it's falling on the players’. It always falls on the players in a performance environment. "In this situation, the decision shouldn't fall on the players because it's not at the player's decision. It was a decision made by the association, by the board and by the executive.

stories.title: O'Gara to stay with La Rochelle until 2031
stories.summary: Ronan O'Gara has officially ended speculation linking him with Leinster by agreeing to remain as head coach of French outfit La Rochelle until 2031. The former Munster out-half had been touted as a potential replacement for Leo Cullen, who will step away from Leinster at the end of the 2026/27 season. However, earlier this month it emerged that discussions between La Rochelle and O'Gara on a fresh contract had started and the club have now announced the news. O'Gara was appointed head coach of the Top 14 side in 2019 - taking sole charge in 2021 - and guided them to European Cup glory in 2022 and '23. "My family and I are very happy and proud to continue this adventure with Stade Rochelais," O'Gara told the club website. "We have lived through exceptional times and gone through more difficult times together. In each of them, I felt the confidence of the Club and the support of our supporters.

stories.title: Zadie Smith to give T. S. Eliot lecture on Sally Rooney at Abbey
stories.summary: British novelist and essayist Zadie Smith is to deliver the 2026 T. S. Eliot Lecture at the Abbey Theatre in Dublin this December. The lecture will return to the Abbey Stage as the eleventh in a series inspired by the influence of poet and writer T. S. Eliot on modern literature. The event is being presented by the T. S. Eliot Estate in association with the Abbey Theatre. This year's lecture is entitled Radical Intimacy: On Sally Rooney, and will focus on the acclaimed Irish author whose novels include Conversations with Friends, Normal People, Beautiful World, Where Are You and Intermezzo. The evening will be introduced by Abbey Theatre Artistic Director Caitríona McLaughlin. Actor Marty Rea will give a reading of T. S. Eliot's Preludes, before Smith takes to the stage to deliver her lecture.

stories.title: Why Louth is the perfect place for a proper escape
stories.summary: Derek O'Connor was invited to visit Louth by Failte Ireland for the purpose of this review. I've always been a fan of the quick getaway. Not the kind that requires several weeks of military planning, a spreadsheet, connecting flights and a minor emotional breakdown somewhere along the way. I'm talking about a proper quick getaway: somewhere gorgeous, somewhere fun and - most importantly - somewhere you can get to without needing a holiday to recover from the holiday. And that’s why Louth is officially a hidden gem. A hop, skip and a jump from the capital and within easy reach of any number of cities, it’s the sort of place that makes you remember exactly why people get so worked up about this whole Ireland thing in the first place. We're talking mountains, loughs, beaches, greenways, history, food and enough fresh air to make you feel positively virtuous before you’ve even had breakfast. Our weekend began in Drogheda, a hub of creativity these days (be sure to check out the splendid Highlanes Gallery), where the town’s streets play host to a rather impressive outdoor art gallery.

stories.title: Cabinet to hear MetroLink cost much higher than estimated
stories.summary: The new estimated cost of building a metro rail system for Dublin, which is being brought to the Cabinet for approval this morning, is expected to be significantly higher than the last estimate for the project four years ago. If Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien gets approval for MetroLink, work could begin on the long-awaited transport project next year. The minister is to outline to his Cabinet colleagues this morning how much its now expected to cost, more than 25 years since the project was announced. When planning permission was submitted in 2022, the Government said the estimated price tag was €9.5 billion, based on costing that put the price range between €7.16bn to and €12.25bn. Since then, construction costs have soared and the new estimate is expected to be significantly higher. If the Cabinet approves the spend, MetroLink can take the next step to a detailed procurement phase, marking one of biggest milestones in the history of the project.

stories.title: EU to outline curbs on children accessing social media
stories.summary: Children and teenagers aged under 15 will not be able to open a social media account without express parental or guardian permission, while those aged under 13 will only be able to access "child friendly" alternatives, under new draft plans set to be outlined by the European Commission president. Ursula von der Leyen's proposal, expected to be called 'EU Kids Act', will be outlined in her annual state of the union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg tomorrow. It will then be further detailed on Thursday by Ms von der Leyen and her colleague Henna Virkkunen, who is the EU's executive vice-president of tech sovereignty, security and democracy. The draft plans are expected to include what is being termed a "block" or "delay" on children and teenagers' access to social media platforms. While a specific age restriction has not yet been finalised, it is expected the draft plan will include four stages: The Irish Government and its counterparts in other EU member states have in recent months emphasised the need for some kind of social media restrictions to be introduced for children and young teens, with an under-16s ban previously mooted.

stories.title: Trump tariff move a late winning goal for Govt at Doonbeg
stories.summary: Irish politics and sport often blend but nothing might replicate Donald Trump's whirlwind 28 hours of golf, diplomacy and trade at the Irish Open in Doonbeg. The US President’s visit to Ireland ended with a major win for the Government, as he used his speech at Shane Lowry’s prizegiving ceremony to announce he would remove tariffs from Irish whiskey. It’s understood that the Taoiseach had raised the issue during his meeting with Mr Trump at Farmleigh House and on a number of occasions over the weekend including at lunch in Doonbeg on Sunday, with Irish whiskey subject to a 10% tariff contrasted to a zero tariff on whiskey coming from Northern Ireland. Government ministers and diplomats could not have dreamed for a better outcome at a time when Ireland’s influence in America has been diminishing and with several of Trump’s administration far from favourable towards the Irish. The announcement – and its ties to Shane Lowry who joked distillers should start sending him cheques – demonstrates how Ireland can use soft diplomacy to punch above its weight at an international level. However, it will be interesting to note the response in Brussels at a time when Ireland is hosting the EU Presidency. The shock tariff announcement will be a boost for Micheál Martin, who has derived a tangible gain from his time in Mr Trump’s company over the weekend.

stories.title: UK inflation hits 3.1%, data offers some relief for BoE
stories.summary: British inflation accelerated to a five-month high of 3.1% in August,but measures excluding surging energy prices held stable, official figures showed today, a day before the Bank of England is expected to keep interest rates on hold. The increase in the annual headline rate was in line with forecasts by economists polled by Reuters, who predicted it would be impacted by the resumption of conflict in the Gulf. Further increases are likely in the coming months when domestic energy bills - which track global market prices with a lag - go up. "Sharp price rises for petrol and diesel pushed inflation up again in August. Higher airfares, particularly for long-haul journeys, also contributed to the increase," Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said. "Rising crude oil and petrol prices increased both the annual cost of raw materials and the price of goods leaving factories respectively," he added. the inflation pickup adds to the headaches of Prime Minister Andy Burnham and finance minister John Healey who have offered voters some support with the cost of living but whose options in a budget plan due on October 28 are limited by the weak state of the public finances.

stories.title: Prince Harry's children move school over security concern
stories.summary: The children of Britain's Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are to swap schools after just two days because of concerns over the security of transporting them, the couple's spokesperson said. Last month, Harry, the younger son of King Charles, and his family relocated to Britain after six years of living in California, with Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, starting school in September. The location of their new home and details of the school have been kept private. However, a spokesperson for the couple confirmed reports that Archie and Lilibet were changing schools after just two days. The distance between their home and the original school, with heavy traffic in the ‌area, had caused concern for ⁠their security team. "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements," the spokesperson said.

stories.title: Iraola and Arteta praise youth after Carabao Cup cameos
stories.summary: Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola praised his young fringe players for their contribution to the 3-1 Carabao Cup third-round win over Tottenham Hotspur. The Basque said the energy of man-of-the-match Lewis Koumas, son of former Tranmere and West Brom midfielder Jason, was "contagious". Koumas, in only his fifth appearance, was deployed as centre-forward with Alexander Isak rested on the bench and the 20-year-old was a constant menace for the Spurs defence in his 86 minutes. But there were also solid performances for 22-year-old James McConnell, in his 14th game, fellow midfielder Trey Nyoni, 19, and winger Rio Ngumoha. "I was happy for them. Different positions, different demands but I think the best thing is they were dead when I subbed them," said Iraola, who made 10 changes from Saturday's flat goalless draw against Fulham. "Trey was cramping, Rio couldn’t have run a lot more. McConnell the same. When this happens, it’s because you’ve given us what you’ve got.
